content: Dosages of Antiretroviral (ARV) Drugs for Adults and Adolescents Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NRTIs) Abacavir (ABC): Administer 300 mg twice daily or 600 mg once daily. Emtricitabine (FTC): Administer 200 mg once daily. Lamivudine (3TC): Administer 150 mg twice daily or 300 mg once daily. Zidovudine (AZT): Administer 300 mg twice daily. Nucleotide Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NtRTIs) Tenofovir Disoproxil Fumarate (TDF): Administer 300 mg once daily. Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF): Administer 10 mg or 25 mg once daily, depending on the regimen. Non-Nucleoside Reverse Transcriptase Inhibitors (NNRTIs) Efavirenz (EFV): Administer 400 mg or 600 mg once daily. Etravirine (ETV): Administer 200 mg twice daily. Nevirapine (NVP): Administer 200 mg once daily for the first 14 days, followed by 200 mg twice daily. Protease Inhibitors (PIs) Atazanavir/Ritonavir (ATV/r): Administer 300 mg/100 mg once daily. Darunavir + Ritonavir (DRV/r): Administer 800 mg + 100 mg once daily or 600 mg + 100 mg twice daily. Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r): Administer 400 mg/100 mg twice daily. Considerations for Individuals Receiving Tuberculosis (TB) Therapy When co-administered with rifampicin, adjust the dose of LPV/r to either 800 mg of LPV + 200 mg of ritonavir twice daily or 400 mg of LPV + 100 mg of ritonavir twice daily with an additional 300 mg of ritonavir twice daily. Close monitoring is required. When co-administered with rifabutin, no dose adjustment is necessary. Rifapentine should not be used in combination with these regimens. Integrase Strand Transfer Inhibitors (INSTIs) Dolutegravir (DTG): Administer 50 mg once daily. Raltegravir (RAL): Administer 400 mg twice daily. Adjustments for TB Therapy with INSTIs When co-administered with rifampicin, increase the dose of DTG to 50 mg twice daily and RAL to 800 mg twice daily. Continue this adjusted dosing for an additional two weeks after the last dose of rifampicin to account for its enzyme-inducing effects. When co-administered with rifabutin or rifapentine, no dose adjustment is required. Pediatric ARV Dosing and Formulations General Considerations Weight-based dosing is preferred for infants and children, as it simplifies implementation and ensures accurate dosing. Fixed-dose combinations (FDCs) are recommended whenever available, as they improve adherence and reduce pill burden. Dispersible tablets are the preferred solid oral dosage form for children, as they can be dissolved in water for easier administration. Oral liquid formulations should be avoided when possible, except for neonatal treatment and prevention, due to challenges in storage, stability, and dosing accuracy. Neonatal and Infant Dosing For neonates younger than two weeks, there is limited pharmacokinetic data to guide accurate dosing for most ARV drugs. Rapid growth and maturation of renal and liver function in this population further complicate dosing. Zidovudine (AZT), Nevirapine (NVP), Lamivudine (3TC), and Abacavir (ABC) have limited pharmacokinetic data for preterm infants, and dosing remains uncertain. Lopinavir/Ritonavir (LPV/r) solution should not be administered to infants younger than two weeks or preterm infants until they reach 42 weeks of gestational age due to the risk of adverse effects. Updates on Dolutegravir (DTG) for Children DTG is approved for children weighing at least 3 kg and aged four weeks or older. For children co-treated with rifampicin-based TB therapy, DTG should be dosed twice daily and continued for two weeks after the last dose of rifampicin. DTG dispersible tablets (10 mg) are not bioequivalent to film-coated tablets (50 mg). A 30 mg dose of dispersible tablets is equivalent to a 50 mg dose of film-coated tablets. Raltegravir (RAL) for Neonates RAL granules were introduced in 2018 to provide a suitable formulation for neonates. However, due to the complexity of administration, dispersible or chewable tablets are preferred for infants and children older than four weeks and weighing at least 3 kg. Simplified Dosing Guidelines for ARV Drugs The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed simplified dosing tables to facilitate the use of ARV drugs in children. These tables prioritize fixed-dose combinations and dispersible tablets to improve adherence and reduce errors. National programs should ensure that ARV products used have received stringent regulatory approval and meet quality and stability standards. Ongoing Research and Updates Studies are ongoing to determine appropriate dosing for children weighing less than 25 kg, particularly for Tenofovir Alafenamide (TAF). Updated guidance will be provided as new data and formulations become available. Recommendations for Program Managers Program managers should ensure the availability of WHO-prequalified ARV drugs and monitor for updates to dosing guidelines as new formulations and data emerge.
